**ARGUMENT**

**I. Defendant Waived Any Right to Compel Arbitration by Substantially Utilizing the Litigation Machinery.**

The right to arbitrate is a contractual right, and like any contractual right it can be waived. This Court has long held that a party waives arbitration by "so substantially utiliz[ing] the litigation machinery that to subsequently permit arbitration would prejudice the party opposing the stay." *Am. Recovery Corp. v. Computerized Thermal Imaging, Inc.*, 96 F.3d 88, 95 (4th Cir. 1996) (citation omitted); *accord MicroStrategy, Inc. v. Lauricia*, 268 F.3d 244, 249–51 (4th Cir. 2001); *Forrester v. Penn Lyon Homes, Inc.*, 553 F.3d 340, 343 (4th Cir. 2009). Waiver is decided by the court. It turns on the party's conduct, not on any secret intent to preserve arbitration. *See Patten Grading & Paving, Inc. v. Skanska USA Bldg., Inc.*, 380 F.3d 200, 204–06 (4th Cir. 2004).

**A. The federal policy favoring arbitration does not shield a litigant who elects the courtroom.**

The Plaintiff will invoke the presumption that doubts about arbitrability are resolved in favor of arbitration. *See Moses H. Cone Mem'l Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp.*, 460 U.S. 1, 24–25 (1983); *Chorley Enters., Inc. v. Dickey's Barbecue Rests., Inc.*, 807 F.3d 553, 562 (4th Cir. 2015). That presumption governs the scope of an arbitration clause. It does not excuse a party's own litigation conduct. Whether a party has waived the right is a question about what that party did, and the Federal Arbitration Act does not relieve a litigant from the consequences of choosing to proceed in court. *See Am. Recovery*, 96 F.3d at 95–96; *see also Rota-McLarty v. Santander Consumer USA, Inc.*, 700 F.3d 690, 700–01 (4th Cir. 2012).

**B. The Plaintiff's conduct is inconsistent with the right to arbitrate.**

Waiver in this Circuit looks to whether the party seeking arbitration has acted inconsistently with that right. The relevant factors include how long the party delayed, what it did in the meantime, and whether it sought relief on the merits. *See MicroStrategy*, 268 F.3d at 249–51; *Patten Grading*, 380 F.3d at 204–06. The Plaintiff's conduct here meets that description. **[Insert record facts: date the complaint was filed; the motions the Plaintiff filed and the relief sought; discovery served or taken; the merits positions advanced; and the date and circumstances of the first demand for arbitration.]** A party that files dispositive motions, takes discovery, and asks the court to rule on the merits has used the court as a forum. It cannot then ask to restart the dispute before an arbitrator if the court's rulings go badly. This Court has treated that kind of delay and merits litigation as the core case for waiver. *See Am. Recovery*, 96 F.3d at 95; *Forrester*, 553 F.3d at 343.

**C. Permitting arbitration now would prejudice Defendant.**

Under this Court's precedents, the dispositive question has been whether the party opposing arbitration has suffered actual prejudice. *Am. Recovery*, 96 F.3d at 95–96. Prejudice is shown where the opposing party has incurred substantial expense in litigation, or where the moving party obtained discovery or tested its arguments in court in ways arbitration would not allow. *See id.*; *Patten Grading*, 380 F.3d at 205–06. **[Insert specifics: fees incurred, discovery produced by Defendant, rulings obtained by Plaintiff, and discovery or procedural advantages Plaintiff would gain in arbitration.]** Defendant has defended this action in the forum Plaintiff chose. Defendant has also disclosed its case, and it would now bear the cost of relitigating the dispute in a second forum.

**D. Waiver is established regardless of prejudice.**

The prejudice requirement no longer controls. The Supreme Court has held that federal courts may not condition waiver of the right to arbitrate on a showing of prejudice. Courts must apply the ordinary waiver rule, which asks whether the party knowingly relinquished the right or acted inconsistently with it. *Morgan v. Sundance, Inc.*, 596 U.S. 411, 419 (2022). To the extent *American Recovery*, *MicroStrategy*, *Patten Grading*, and *Forrester* make prejudice an element, they have been abrogated on that point. Their description of the conduct that amounts to waiver is still instructive. Under *Morgan*, Defendant need not prove prejudice. Plaintiff's litigation conduct, set out above, is inconsistent with an intent to arbitrate and is enough to establish waiver. In any event, the prejudice described above independently satisfies the former standard.

The Court should hold that Plaintiff waived any right to compel arbitration and should affirm the denial of its motion.
